activities.anchor: Each force presses on the price-cost
activities.caption: pair each force with the side of the margin it squeezes
activities.name: scForcesMatch

config.prompt: Five forces, five pressures — pair each with how it presses on the margin:

pairs.right: squeeze prices or demand costly features
cap the price you can charge at all
erupts into fare wars on every route

config.why: Rivalry is only one of five: industry structure, not managerial effort, sets the profit pool — and each force presses from a different side.

activities.anchor: Compare US scheduled airlines with soft-drink concentrate
activities.caption: drag the divider — two industries, one question
activities.name: scAirlineCompare

config.prompt: Same effort, different structure — drag the divider:

before.label: scheduled airlines
before.text: Planes leased, so entry is easy; a commodity seat with zero switching costs and price-comparison sites arming every buyer; concentrated suppliers; demand swings with the economy — rivalry erupts into fare wars. Economics hover near break-even.

after.label: soft-drink concentrate
after.text: Two dominant brands whose rivalry settled into non-price competition; customers loyal for life; franchised bottlers with little bargaining power. Spectacular returns, for decades.

config.why: The gap is not about effort, intelligence or management quality — structure tells you in advance, which is Buffett's joke about shooting down the Wright brothers at Kitty Hawk.

activities.anchor: quadruple the sample merely to halve the error
activities.caption: call the precision budget
activities.name: scSampleEstimate

config.prompt: A random sample of 1,000 respondents — roughly what margin of error should you quote at 95% confidence?
config.why: The 1/√n rule: 1,000 gives about ±3.2, 400 gives ±5 — and quadrupling the sample merely halves the error, which is why the strategist decides which questions deserve the money.
config.context: A manager demanding ±1% certainty is ordering a 10,000-person study — the alternative is 12 sharp customer interviews.

activities.anchor: Porter's generic strategies say there are only two coherent ways
activities.caption: choose the position, take the mix that follows
activities.name: scPositionBranch

config.root: You compete across a broad market. Porter says there are only two coherent ways to beat the industry average — choose, then live with the mix it implies.

start.text: The board asks for the position. What do you choose?

choices.label: Cost leadership — acceptably good at structurally lower cost
choices.feedback: Your 4Ps follow: high-volume no-frills distribution, promotion built on price and availability, a deliberately narrow range.

choices.label: Differentiation — a product buyers pay a premium for
choices.feedback: Your 4Ps follow: brand, channels and service that a cost leader would call waste.

choices.label: Focus — one of the two, on a narrow underserved segment
choices.feedback: Valid third option — but you still owe the segment a coherent mix of one of the two kinds.

cost.text: A rival proposes premium packaging for one product line. Response?

choices.label: Refuse — it dilutes the cost system
choices.feedback: That refusal is the strategy: every P either reinforces the position or quietly betrays it.

choices.label: Try it — the brand could use the lift
choices.feedback: Premium pricing without premium differentiation is the first step to stuck-in-the-middle.

diff.text: A rival undercuts you 20% on a me-too product. Response?

choices.label: Deepen the differentiation, hold the premium
choices.feedback: The premium is earned by the mix, not the price list — defend it there.

choices.label: Match the price
choices.feedback: Full costs without premium prices — the other road into the middle.

focus.text: The narrow segment rewards the position the broad players underserve — commit fully to one of the two kinds of mix.

coherent.text: A coherent system of trade-offs: the refusals are the moat's foundation.

middle.text: Stuck-in-the-middle: neither identity bought, both costs paid.

config.why: A cost leader's mix is not 'the same marketing, done cheaper' — the position and the mix stand or fall together.

activities.caption: one line of the trade-off logic is wrong
activities.name: scTradeoffSpot

config.prompt: One line of this Southwest trade-off summary is wrong. Find it.
lines: Southwest runs point-to-point, no meals, no assigned seats, one aircraft type
A full-service rival could copy any single choice tomorrow
Copying the whole system strands the rival's own hubs, crews and frequent-flyer machine
So the rival copies the system and keeps its own position intact
Strategy is the set of things you deliberately refuse to do
config.correction: So the rival must abandon its own position to copy — imitation is self-destructive, which is what defends the position.
config.why: A position is defensible only as a system of trade-offs: without them nothing stops an equal rival from doing exactly what you do, and the profit is borrowed, not owned.

activities.caption: file the examples by the moat they ride on
activities.name: scMoatBuckets

config.prompt: Seven structures protect a position. File each example:

items.label: n users hold n × (n − 1) / 2 possible connections
an ERP replacement costing a year of retraining
patents and licences with legal clocks

config.why: Note what is not on the list: technology alone, being first, or market share — share in a structurally bad industry is just a bigger share of the losses.

activities.anchor: Entrants launch a product that is worse
activities.caption: which curve is the low-end entrant?
activities.name: scDisruptTrace

config.prompt: Mainstream criteria on the vertical axis, time on the horizontal. Which curve is the low-end entrant's trajectory?

curves.label: A: starts below, improves along its own axis

config.why: Worse by the incumbents' best customers' criteria — then improving until it meets mainstream demand at a cost structure the incumbent cannot match: minimills, PCs, streaming, digital photography.

activities.anchor: an espresso machine and a lease
activities.caption: fill the blanks — score the two industries
activities.name: scForcesCloze

config.text: Coffee shop: entry barriers are %%0%%, so new-entrant threat scores %%1%%, and every street has substitutes. Valve distributor: buyers who spec valves into million-pound projects face %%2%% costs and qualification processes to switch, so buyer power scores low.
config.hint: One industry is structurally hostile; the other is an attractive niche hiding in an unglamorous industry.
